summary: Specifies BRSKI, an automated process for securely bootstrapping a new device into a network. It uses manufacturer-installed X.509 certificates together with a manufacturer's authorizing service, which can be online or offline, to set up a key infrastructure without manual configuration.

plainLanguage.summary: Bootstrapping Remote Secure Key Infrastructure (BRSKI) lets a factory-fresh device join a network by itself. The device proves who it is with a certificate burned in at the factory. The network's registrar then asks the manufacturer to sign a voucher that gives the device the network's identity and permission to join.

questions: how to securely onboard a new network device
how does a pledge get a voucher
what is a masa in brski
what does brski ask the manufacturer for
subtitle: How a brand-new device proves who it is, learns who owns it, and joins a network with no manual setup.

tldr.problem: A new network device cannot build a secure connection on its own, and asking an operator to load keys by hand does not scale.
tldr.mechanism: The device carries a certificate installed by its manufacturer and presents it to the network's registrar. The registrar asks the manufacturer for a signed voucher that both permits the transfer of control and carries the trust anchor the device should believe from then on.
tldr.outcome: The device ends up holding a real key infrastructure identity, having talked only to the registrar and the manufacturer. The whole exchange is logged, so a later owner can check what happened before it accepts the device.

today: RFC 8995 is a Proposed Standard on the IETF Standards Track and has not been obsoleted or updated. It defines the bootstrap protocol used by the ANIMA autonomic control plane, and it builds on the voucher artifact defined in RFC 8366 and the enrollment protocol defined in RFC 7030.

sections.title: Bootstrapping a Device Without Help
sections.content:
The Bootstrapping Remote Secure Key Infrastructure (BRSKI) protocol automates the secure enrolment of new, unconfigured devices, which the document calls pledges. A pledge carries an Initial Device Identifier (IDevID), an X.509 certificate installed by the manufacturer at the factory, and nothing more.

The document's premise is that a device cannot build a secure relationship on its own. The first connection to a network has to rest on something put in place before the device was ever plugged in, namely the manufacturer's own certificate.

Bootstrapping can happen with a routable address and a cloud service, with only link-local connectivity, or on limited or disconnected networks. The document also covers deployment models with less stringent security requirements. Bootstrapping is complete when the cryptographic identity of the new key infrastructure has been deployed to the device.
sections.plainLanguage: BRSKI lets a brand-new device join a network by itself. The device proves who it is with a certificate burned in at the factory, and the network's owner asks the manufacturer for permission to take it.

sections.title: The Parties and Their Roles
sections.content:
Four parties take part. The pledge is the device trying to join. The join proxy gives the pledge the HTTPS connectivity it needs to reach the network, and the pledge is unaware that it is talking to a proxy rather than straight to the registrar. The domain registrar is the network's decision maker: it authenticates the pledge, decides whether to accept it, and passes vouchers back to it. The manufacturer service, acting as a Manufacturer Authorized Signing Authority (MASA), issues the vouchers that say a device may be owned by this domain.

The domain is the managed network the pledge is joining: the proxy, the registrar, the domain certificate authority and the management components, all sharing a common local trust anchor. The document assumes a multivendor network, where each manufacturer may run its own service or an integrator may run one authorised by several manufacturers.
sections.plainLanguage: Four parties help a device join. The device asks a local helper for a path to the network. The network's registrar decides whether to accept it. The manufacturer signs the permission slip that lets the device trust the registrar.

sections.title: The Pledge's Five Steps
sections.content:
The pledge moves through five steps. It discovers a channel to a registrar, using GRASP or mDNS on the local link. It identifies itself by presenting its IDevID certificate in a TLS handshake, during which the registrar's certificate is only provisionally accepted. It then requests to join, including a unique nonce so that any response can be tied to this particular attempt. Next it imprints on the registrar, which means verifying the manufacturer's voucher and the trust anchor it carries. Finally it enrolls, obtaining a certificate from the domain over the now fully authenticated TLS session.

A pledge that is rejected returns to discovery. A pledge that gets a bad response from the manufacturer goes back one step. An enrollment failure sends it back to imprint. Once enrolled, the device repeats only the discovery step if it is returned to factory default settings.
sections.plainLanguage: The device works through five steps: find a registrar, show its factory certificate, ask to join, check the manufacturer's permission slip, and collect a certificate from the network. Any step can send it back to the start.

sections.title: Vouchers and Secure Imprinting
sections.content:
A voucher is a cryptographically protected artifact, signed by the manufacturer, that authorises a zero-touch imprint on the registrar's domain. Its format and cryptographic mechanism are defined in RFC 8366. The pledge imprints only when it can validate a voucher, and the voucher carries the trust anchor the pledge will use to represent its owner.

The document frames the protocol as the answer to four questions. The registrar authenticates the pledge: who is this device and what is its identity. The registrar authorises the pledge: is it mine, do I want it, and what are the chances it has been compromised. The pledge authenticates the registrar: what is this registrar's identity. The pledge authorises the registrar: should I join this network. The IDevID and a TLS connection answer the first two; the voucher answers the last two.
sections.plainLanguage: The manufacturer's signed permission slip is called a voucher. It carries the certificate the device should trust from then on. The device accepts the network only when that slip checks out.

sections.title: The Voucher-Request Artifact
sections.content:
A voucher-request is a small extension to the voucher format defined in RFC 8366. It carries the information the manufacturer needs to decide whether a registrar may claim a device: the device's serial number and the identity that signed its IDevID. The pledge signs it with the credentials in its IDevID, and the registrar signs the copy it forwards to the manufacturer.

BRSKI uses JSON for all new operations and for voucher formats, and carries binary values in base64. A voucher that comes back holds the nonce, the assertion method, a pinned-domain-cert and the serial number, plus an expiry for a nonceless voucher. The recommended lifetime for a nonceless voucher is on the order of 20 minutes, long enough to finish the provisional phase and no longer.
sections.plainLanguage: The request is a small signed JSON document. It names the device and says who signed for it. The answer is a similar document that also carries the certificate the device should trust from then on.

sections.title: The Protocol in Detail
sections.content:
Two channels carry the protocol. BRSKI-EST runs between the pledge and the registrar, and BRSKI-MASA runs between the registrar and the manufacturer. Both live under the /.well-known/brski URI tree. The pledge asks for a voucher with an HTTPS POST to /.well-known/brski/requestvoucher, and the registrar later asks the manufacturer for the audit log at /.well-known/brski/requestauditlog.

The TLS session between the pledge and the registrar starts in a provisional state. The pledge accepts the registrar's certificate without checking it, because it has no way to check it yet, and it must treat everything it receives as untrusted until a voucher has been verified. TLS 1.2 or newer is required on the pledge side, and TLS 1.3 is encouraged. The pledge sends a nonce and the voucher must carry the same nonce, which proves the voucher is fresh and belongs to this attempt.

The registrar checks the manufacturer's audit log before it accepts the voucher, and the pledge reports the outcome of voucher parsing back to the registrar as status telemetry. The device then uses the authenticated session to enrol with the domain's certificate authority over EST, which is the point where the single pinned trust anchor grows into a full local key infrastructure.
sections.plainLanguage: The device talks to the network's registrar, and the manufacturer talks to the registrar. The first exchange is not yet trusted, so the device checks everything carefully until the voucher proves the connection is genuine.

sections.title: Privacy Considerations
sections.content:
The manufacturer sees the device serial number and the identity that signed the IDevID, and it records the domain identity of every domain it issues a voucher to. A privacy-sensitive domain can keep much of that private. The domainID captures only the unauthenticated subject key identifier of the domain, so a domain that generates a new domainID for each device deployed, and buys devices from a manufacturer that does not require sales channel integration, gains a significant level of privacy while keeping the audit-log inspection the registrar relies on.

The provisional exchange also leaks something. TLS 1.2 reveals the certificate identities to anyone on the path, including the join proxy. TLS 1.3 reveals them only to the end parties, but an attacker in the middle of the provisional connection can still see them. Any device that can see a join proxy could connect to the registrar and learn the identity of the network, and pseudonymizing the registrar's certificate would still allow connections in different places to be correlated. The document judges this unlikely to matter for the ANIMA use case, but a concern for other users.
sections.plainLanguage: The manufacturer learns which device is being claimed and which network is claiming it. The registrar's certificate identity is also visible during the first, untrusted exchange. Networks that care about this have ways to limit what the manufacturer sees.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The document describes a protocol that balances operational needs against security. Reduced security modes are possible, and Section 7 lists them as non-normative design guidance: a pledge may be programmed to skip voucher validation once, a registrar may accept devices without authenticating them, and a device may accept nonceless vouchers so that it can be deployed when the manufacturer service is unreachable. The security of the protocol then rests on logging and on the registrar's audit checks.

Against denial of service against the manufacturer service, a registrar can keep long-term copies of nonceless vouchers. That creates the opposite risk: a previous owner who intercepts traffic can use a previously issued nonceless voucher to regain control of a device it has sold. The mitigation is that every issuance is recorded in the manufacturer's audit log, which the next registrar verifies, and that pledges only bootstrap from a factory default state.

During the provisional period the pledge must treat all HTTP header and content data as untrusted. The domainID must be resistant to second-preimage attacks, and good random numbers are needed. If several registrars claim the same device at once, several vouchers may be issued, and the pledge picks one; the registrars see the duplicate entries in the log and take them into account.
sections.plainLanguage: The protocol has weaker modes for emergency and offline use, and the document says so. The safety net is the manufacturer's log of every voucher it has issued, which the next owner can check before trusting a device.

items.title: Pledge
items.text: The unconfigured device trying to join. It carries a factory-installed IDevID certificate.

items.title: Join proxy
items.text: Gives the device the connectivity it needs to reach the registrar. The device does not know it is talking to a proxy.

items.title: Domain registrar
items.text: Authenticates the device, decides whether to accept it, and hands back the voucher.

items.title: Manufacturer service
items.text: Acts as a Manufacturer Authorized Signing Authority (MASA) and signs the vouchers.
